sentences.text: Herrerasaurus measured about 6 meters in length and weighed approximately 350 kilograms.
Adult individuals reached a total length of up to 6 meters, a skull length of 56 centimeters, and a weight of 350 kilograms.
The creature moved on two legs exclusively.
It displays traits found in different groups of dinosaurs and non-dinosaurian archosaurs, sharing most dinosaur characteristics but differing in hip and leg bone shapes.
A specific skull specimen bears bite pits on the bone and splenial, with surrounding tissue suggesting a short-lived non-lethal infection likely from a fight with another individual.
Fossilized coprolites attributed to this predator contain small bones but no plant fragments, indicating it could digest bones.
The genus Herrerasaurus was first described by Osvaldo Reig in 1963.
The name means "Herrera's lizard" and honors the rancher who found the first specimen in 1958.
The holotype specimen PVL 2566 was found in the Cancha de Bochas Member of the Ischigualasto Formation in San Juan, Argentina.
Osvaldo Reig named the dinosaur after Victorino Herrera, a goatherd who discovered fossils near San Juan, Argentina, in 1959.
Herrerasaurus was a carnivore that preyed on small and medium-sized plant eaters based on its teeth and size.
Dental microwear patterns suggest Herrerasaurus may have swallowed small prey whole with minimal oral processing, similar to modern crocodylians.
Coprolites found in the Ischigualasto Formation containing small bones but no plant fragments are assigned to Herrerasaurus, indicating it could digest bone.
Herrerasaurus was a carnivore that hunted small to medium-sized animals based on its teeth and size.
Herrerasaurus may have preyed on other dinosaurs, including the herbivore Pisanosaurus.
Because dinosaurs were rare during its time, Herrerasaurus likely included abundant rhynchosaurs and herbivorous synapsids in its diet.
A specimen of Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis had a cranial bone incision attributed to a bite by Paul Sereno and Fernando Novas.
Two additional holes in the splenial bone showed swelling and porosity, suggesting a short-duration non-lethal infection.
Based on the size and angle of the wounds, it is probable they were inflicted during a fight with another Herrerasaurus.
Herrerasaurus belongs to the family Herrerasauridae, which includes some of the earliest genera in the dinosaur evolutionary radiation.
Herrerasaurus was originally classified within Carnosauria, a group that included animals similar to Megalosaurus and Antrodemus.
Potential members of the Herrerasauridae clade may include Chindesaurus from Arizona and possibly Caseosaurus from Texas, though their relationships are not fully understood.
All known fossils of Herrerasaurus come from the Ischigualasto Formation in northwestern Argentina, dating to the Carnian stage of the Late Triassic approximately 231.4 million years ago.
The sediments containing the holotype were deposited during the Carnian stage of the Triassic, approximately 231 to 229 million years ago.
Herrerasaurus lived during the Carnian stage of the Late Triassic, approximately 231.4 million years ago.
Vegetation included ferns, horsetails, and giant conifers.

Herrerasaurus lived in Late Triassic South American jungles alongside early dinosaurs like Sanjuansaurus and Eoraptor, as well as rhynchosaurs, cynodonts, dicynodonts, pseudosuchians, proterochampsids, and temnospondyls.
There is a persistent scientific debate over whether Herrerasaurus is a primitive theropod or a basal saurischian, with different researchers supporting each view.
If Herrerasaurus is a theropod, it suggests that theropods, sauropodomorphs, and ornithischians diverged before the middle Carnian and independently evolved features like advanced ankle joints.
Ichnological records of large three-toed footprints from the early Carnian Los Rastros Formation support the hypothesis that Herrerasaurus was a theropod.

Gregory Paul suggested Staurikosaurus pricei was incorrectly identified as a juvenile Herrerasaurus, but this was refuted when young Herrerasaurus pelvic bones were found to lack resemblance to Staurikosaurus pelvis.
